case_name: Workplace Sexual Harassment - Vishakha Guidelines Compliance
scenario: A female software engineer filed a complaint against her team lead for persistent sexual harassment including inappropriate messages, unwanted physical contact, and quid pro quo demands. The company's Internal Complaints Committee (ICC) dismissed the complaint citing 'insufficient evidence'.
facts: The engineer documented harassment over 6 months including WhatsApp messages, witnesses who saw inappropriate behavior, and instances of career retaliation when she rejected advances. The ICC consisted only of male members and did not follow proper inquiry procedures.
legal_issues: Sexual harassment at workplace under POSH Act
Proper constitution and functioning of ICC
applicable_laws: Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013
judgment: The court held the company liable for failing to comply with POSH Act requirements. The ICC was improperly constituted (must have external member and 50% women members). The inquiry was procedurally flawed. The court ordered: 1) Fresh inquiry by properly constituted ICC, 2) Interim relief including transfer of harasser, 3) Compensation of 6 months salary, 4) Company to undergo compliance audit, 5) Criminal proceedings against harasser under IPC 354A.
key_principles: All workplaces with 10+ employees must have ICC
ICC must have 50% women members and one external member
Burden of proof shifts to accused in POSH cases
Company liable for not taking complaints seriously
Digital evidence (WhatsApp, emails) is admissible and strong evidence
Retaliation against complainant is punishable offense
Compensation can include mental agony, loss of career opportunity
precedents: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) - Landmark case establishing guidelines
Medha Kotwal Lele v. Union of India (2013) - POSH Act enforcement
Apparel Export Promotion Council v. A.K. Chopra (1999)
practical_advice: Document all instances of harassment immediately
Save digital evidence (messages, emails, screenshots)
File written complaint with ICC within 3 months (extendable to 6 months)
Request interim relief (transfer, leave) during inquiry
ICC inquiry must complete within 90 days
Complainant can bring support person to ICC proceedings
If ICC fails, can approach police and file FIR
Company must display POSH Act provisions prominently
Annual compliance reports are mandatory
Know your rights - harassment includes verbal, physical, digital conduct

case_name: Remote Work and Work From Home Rights Post-Pandemic
scenario: After 2 years of successful remote work during pandemic, company mandated full return to office. An employee with medical condition requested permanent WFH as reasonable accommodation but was denied and threatened with termination.
facts: The employee, a software engineer with chronic health condition, worked remotely with excellent performance ratings. Post-pandemic, company issued blanket return-to-office policy without considering individual circumstances. Employee provided medical certificates supporting WFH request.
legal_issues: Right to work from home in post-pandemic era
Reasonable accommodation for employees with disabilities
applicable_laws: Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 - Section 20, 21
Constitution of India - Article 14 (Equality), 21 (Right to life)
judgment: The court ruled partially in favor of the employee. While employers generally have right to determine work location, they must: 1) Provide reasonable accommodation for persons with disabilities, 2) Consider individual circumstances in good faith, 3) Not discriminate based on health conditions. The court ordered: a) Permanent WFH arrangement for the employee with periodic review, b) Company to develop formal WFH policy with objective criteria, c) Compensation for mental harassment.
key_principles: Employers must provide reasonable accommodation for disabilities
Unilateral change in fundamental employment terms requires consent
Medical evidence supporting WFH creates obligation to consider
Post-pandemic, WFH is recognized as viable work arrangement
Blanket policies without individual consideration may be discriminatory
Performance track record relevant in WFH requests
Constructive dismissal occurs when conditions made untenable
precedents: National Federation of the Blind v. Union of India (2013) - Disability rights
Jeeja Ghosh v. Union of India (2016) - Reasonable accommodation
Samta Andolan Samiti v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2017)
practical_advice: Request WFH accommodation in writing with medical evidence
Document performance achievements during remote work period
Propose hybrid arrangement as compromise if needed
Companies should have formal WFH/hybrid policies
Disability accommodation is legal right, not favor
Keep all communications regarding WFH requests
If denied, file grievance through internal channels first
Consider disability discrimination complaint if applicable
Many IT companies now offer permanent hybrid options
Negotiate WFH as part of employment terms for new jobs

case_name: Notice Period Buyout and Immediate Resignation
scenario: An engineer wanted to join a new company immediately but was required to serve 3-month notice period. The employee offered to pay 3 months salary as buyout but employer refused and threatened legal action if employee left.
facts: Employment contract stated 90-day notice period or payment of equivalent salary. Employee had urgent family reasons to relocate. Employer refused buyout citing critical project and 'unrecoverable losses'. Employee resigned and left, depositing 3 months salary with labor court.
legal_issues: Right to buy out notice period
Employer's right to refuse notice buyout
applicable_laws: Shops and Establishments Act - Notice period regulations
Constitution of India - Article 23 (Prohibition of forced labor)
judgment: The court held in favor of the employee. Key findings: 1) Notice period buyout clause is essentially liquidated damages, 2) If employee pays equivalent salary, employer cannot refuse and insist on service, 3) Forcing employee to serve against will violates Article 23, 4) Employer failed to prove actual loss exceeding 3 months salary, 5) Contract terms must be reasonable and not amount to servitude. The court dismissed employer's suit and ordered return of deposited amount to employee with interest.
key_principles: Employer cannot force employee to serve notice period if buyout is paid
Notice period buyout is liquidated damages, not optional
Long notice periods (3 months) are enforceable only for specific roles
Employer must prove actual damages exceeding liquidated amount
Forcing service against will violates fundamental rights
Payment in lieu of notice must be accepted by employer
Contract cannot create involuntary servitude
precedents: Central Inland Water Transport Corporation Ltd. v. Brojo Nath Ganguly (1986)
Delhi Transport Corporation v. D.T.C. Mazdoor Congress (1991)
ONGC v. Offshore Pipeline Contractors (1994) - Liquidated damages
practical_advice: Notice period buyout is your right if provided in contract
Employer generally cannot refuse buyout payment
Keep written proof of resignation and buyout offer
90 days is common in IT, but enforceability depends on circumstances
Negotiate shorter notice period in employment contract
Some companies have clauses to recover training costs - check contract
If employer refuses buyout unreasonably, consult lawyer
New employer should provide joining buffer for notice period
Document handover activities to show good faith
Notice period cannot be indefinite or unreasonable

case_name: Mental Health Leave and Workplace Stress
scenario: A software engineer suffered severe depression and anxiety due to workplace stress, excessive work hours, and hostile management. The employee requested medical leave but was denied and threatened with performance action.
facts: The employee worked 70-80 hour weeks consistently, received abusive messages from manager, and developed clinical depression requiring psychiatric treatment. Doctor certified 30-day rest. Company denied leave citing 'business needs' and started performance review.
legal_issues: Right to medical leave for mental health
Disability discrimination for mental health conditions
Constructive dismissal through impossible work conditions
Duty of care owed by employer
applicable_laws: Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 (mental illness is disability)
Factories Act, 1948 - Worker health and safety
Shops and Establishments Act - Medical leave provisions
Constitution of India - Article 21 (Right to health)
judgment: The court ruled strongly in favor of the employee. Mental health is equally protected as physical health under law. Employer's denial of legitimate medical leave is illegal and amounts to disability discrimination. The excessive work hours and hostile environment violated duty of care. The court ordered: 1) Immediate grant of 30-day medical leave with pay, 2) Abandonment of performance review, 3) Compensation for mental harassment (Rs. 5 lakhs), 4) Mandatory mental health policy implementation, 5) Psychological counseling support.
key_principles: Mental health leave has same legal status as physical health leave
Mental illness is recognized as disability requiring accommodation
Employer has duty of care for employee mental wellbeing
Excessive work hours creating health issues is actionable
Medical certificates for mental health must be honored
Retaliation for taking mental health leave is illegal
Workplace stress causing clinical condition = employer liability
precedents: Food Corporation of India v. Smt. Ved Prakash Gupta (1990) - Mental health disability
Air India v. Nergesh Meerza (1981) - Health rights of employees
State of Punjab v. Jagir Singh (2015) - Mental fitness
practical_advice: Mental health is valid medical reason for leave
Get proper medical certification from psychiatrist/psychologist
Mental Healthcare Act 2017 protects rights of persons with mental illness
Employer cannot discriminate based on mental health condition
Document excessive work hours and toxic workplace conditions
Many companies now have EAP (Employee Assistance Programs)
Request reasonable accommodation for mental health conditions
Workplace stress causing illness can lead to compensation claims
Know your leave entitlements - privilege, sick, casual leave
If denied, file complaint with HR and labor authorities
Seek professional help without fear of job loss

case_name: Variable Pay and Performance Bonus Disputes
scenario: A senior engineer was promised 30% variable pay based on performance. Despite excellent ratings and achievement of all KPIs, company paid only 10% citing 'business losses' and 'discretionary nature' of bonus.
facts: Offer letter stated 'up to 30% variable pay based on performance'. Annual review rated employee 4.5/5. All measurable targets exceeded. Company made profit that year but paid minimal bonus citing 'discretion' and 'performance linkage'.
legal_issues: Interpretation of 'up to' clauses in compensation
Unfair labor practice in bonus denial
applicable_laws: Indian Contract Act, 1872 - Interpretation of contracts
judgment: The court analyzed the employment contract and company's bonus policy. While 'up to 30%' gives some discretion, it cannot be illusory. When employee achieves excellent performance (documented), reduction to 10% without valid business reason is arbitrary. Company's profitability that year negated 'business loss' argument. The court ordered: 1) Payment of 25% variable pay (reasonable given performance), 2) Interest on delayed payment, 3) Clarification of bonus policy for future transparency.
key_principles: 'Discretionary' bonus becomes contractual when systematically promised
Excellent performance creates legitimate expectation of promised variable pay
Company cannot arbitrarily reduce variable pay without valid reasons
'Up to X%' means genuine possibility of X%, not just 0-X%
Business losses must be genuine and documented to reduce variable pay
Contractual terms must be applied consistently and fairly
Employer cannot use 'discretion' to deny earned compensation
precedents: Bridge & Roof Co. Ltd. v. Union of India (1963) - Bonus as deferred wage
Associated Cement Companies Ltd. v. P.N. Sharma (1965)
Workmen of Nilgiri Coop. Marketing Society v. State of TN (2004)
practical_advice: Get variable pay terms in writing in offer letter
Understand difference between discretionary and guaranteed bonus
Document all performance achievements and KPIs met
Request clear, measurable criteria for variable pay calculation
'Up to X%' should realistically pay X% for excellent performance
Ask for transparency in bonus calculation methodology
Compare with peers who received full variable pay
Bonus Act applies only to employees earning below threshold
For high earners, contract terms govern variable pay
If systematically promised and paid, bonus becomes contractual right
Raise dispute through HR and labor commissioner if denied unfairly
